caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: CRCNS:bst-3
attempts.entry_title: Brainstem networks for threat probability and prediction error (Strickland and McDannald 2022)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings held up in this data, using the paper's own cluster membership from its Source Data. Cue clusters ordered by threat probability, the cue subnetwork carrying threat probability and behaviour signals, positive prediction error coding, and the shock and prediction error signals of the outcome networks reproduced. The link between faster danger responses and larger contribution to the threat signal did not (R2 = 0.067), as the paper's latencies do not follow its stated method and no script computes them. The cue hubs, the subnetwork lesion and the separation of the outcome networks held only in part; the networks separate with squared correlations but not with Pearson r. Every claim could be tested.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Strickland and McDannald (2022) on CRCNS data set bst-3, which holds 1812 brainstem single units recorded with Neuropixels in ten rats during probabilistic fear discrimination, the cube file of binned and normalized firing built from them, and the paper's MATLAB scripts. It checks the behaviour, the unit counts, the k-means clusters and their PCA, the regression and lesion analyses of threat probability, behaviour, shock and prediction error signals, and the anatomy of the networks, with the paper's own cluster membership taken from its Source Data.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Strickland and McDannald (2022) from CRCNS bst-3

outcomes.statement: The data set's units can be matched to the rows of the paper's Source Data cluster sheets, which gives the paper's own cue and outcome cluster membership.
outcomes.source: Source Data, sheets Figure 2b k1 to k21 and Figure 4b k1 to k11; Supplementary Methods, Z-score normalization and K-means clustering
outcomes.notes: Under the normalization of the paper's cubeScript.m (the data set's cube), every one of the 1812 cue rows and 1812 outcome rows of the Source Data cluster sheets equals exactly one unit's row (largest difference 5e-15), so 100% match and every unit gets one cue and one outcome cluster, with the sizes the claims file lists. Under the claims file's four readings (n-a, n-b, w-a, w-b, computed from the spike times in 250-ms bins) at most 2 rows match within 0.01, though 1664 cue rows and 650 to 1728 outcome rows correlate above 0.99 with a unit.
deviations: The rows that match are normalized as cubeScript.m does (firing in 1-s and 500-ms bins over the 40 s from 10 s before cue onset, minus the trial's 2-s pre-cue rate rounded down, z-scored over all trials and bins at each bin size), a detail the Supplementary Methods describe differently (250-ms bins averaged, other windows) and the paper's code settles. The claims file's four readings are shown and none matches.

outcomes.statement: During recording sessions suppression of rewarded nose poking was high to danger, intermediate to uncertainty and low to safety, with a main effect of cue (F(2,142) = 149.2, p = 1.26 x 10^-35) over 73 sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1c; Source Data Fig. 1c
outcomes.quote: Suppression of rewarded nose poking was high to danger, intermediate to uncertainty, and low to safety (Fig. 1c ; ANOVA main effect of cue [ F (2,142) = 149.2, p = 1.26 × 10 –35 ]
outcomes.notes: 73 sessions. With empty trials set to 1 (cubeScript.m) the means are 0.914, 0.709 and 0.230, equal to Source Data Fig. 1c, and every session's values equal a Source Data row. Cue x sex mixed ANOVA (a-a) F(2,142) = 147.9, p < 1e-30. With empty trials set to 0 (sr-a) F = 145.6, left out (sr-b) F = 150.4. The repeated-measures reading (a-b) gives F(2,144) = 116.2. 31 of 1168 trials had no pokes in either period.
deviations: Empty trials are set to 1 as cubeScript.m does (poke.SR(isnan(poke.SR)) = 1), a detail the Methods leave open; the claims file's sr-a and sr-b are shown and give the same order and an F within tolerance.

outcomes.statement: Rats showed complete discrimination during the recording sessions, shown rat by rat with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Supplementary Fig. 2 legend
outcomes.quote: Rats showed complete discrimination during recording sessions
outcomes.notes: Under reading c-c all 8 rats with at least 3 sessions have danger and uncertainty suppression intervals that exclude zero. Under c-a 7 of 8 (subject 9's uncertainty minus safety interval is -0.06 to 0.28) and under c-b 5 of 8. Subjects 4 and 6 (2 sessions and 1) have means ordered danger > uncertainty > safety.
deviations: The legend does not say which quantity's interval is tested; three readings are run and the claim holds under c-c.

outcomes.statement: 1812 single units were isolated and held over 73 one-hour sessions from ten rats, 965 of them from the four females, with per-subject totals of 192, 328, 141, 32, 52, 43, 116, 195, 409 and 304 units (subjects 1 to 10).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Supplementary Tables 1 and 2
outcomes.quote: We isolated and held 1812 neurons during 73, 1-h recording sessions (965 neurons from the 4 females, Supplementary Table S1 )
outcomes.notes: Subjects mapped from animal ids as cueAnalysis.m does (js10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 21, 22, 24, 25, 27 to 1 to 10; js10, 11, 13 and 27 female). All counts equal the paper's. Supplementary Table 1 lists 75 sessions; the data set has 7 for subject 5 (8 listed) and 9 for subject 10 (10 listed).

outcomes.statement: The units spanned 21 brainstem regions, from the deep gray layer of the superior colliculus to the median raphe, with the largest counts in the paramedian raphe (236), ventral dorsal raphe (208) and dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (179).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1d and 1e; Supplementary Table 2; Source Data Fig. 3e left
outcomes.quote: Neurons spanned 21 brainstem regions 13 (Fig. 1d ), including subregions and neighboring regions of the superior colliculus, periaqueductal gray, dorsal raphe, and median raphe
outcomes.notes: 21 regions hold units after the scripts' merges (region 21, CIC, into DpWh; 24 into x/scp), and every region's count equals the sum of Source Data Fig. 3e left.
deviations: Region names and merges come from cubeScript.m and cueAnalysis.m; the cube's own region strings are MATLAB string objects that cannot be read outside MATLAB.

outcomes.statement: K-means clustering of cue firing organized brainstem neurons into at least 21 functional clusters, of sizes from 24 to 219 (median 83).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 2b; Supplementary Methods, K-means clustering
outcomes.quote: K-means clustering for mean, single-unit firing in 1-s bins from 2-s prior to 2-s following cue presentation (danger, uncertainty, and safety) revealed neurons could be organized into at least 21 functional clusters ... Cluster size varied (min size = 24, max = 219, and median = 83)
outcomes.notes: Medians over 20 k-means seeds (k-means++ seeding, one replicate) of the smallest, largest and median cluster sizes are 24.0, 218.5 and 75.0, all within tolerance (the median near the lower edge, 74.7). Single seeds give 14 to 38, 171 to 274 and 63 to 93. The paper's clustering has a summed squared distance of 11219, inside the seeds' range (11135 to 11336).
deviations: The script seeds MATLAB's generator (rng(1)), which cannot be repeated in Python; 20 seeds are used, as the claims file's standard choice says.

outcomes.statement: Across all 1812 neurons, the first principal component of cue firing (29.7% of firing variance) was ordered cue firing, danger > uncertainty > safety.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 2c inset
outcomes.quote: Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed ordered cue firing (danger > uncertainty > safety) to be the primary low-dimensional feature across all brainstem neurons (PC1, explaining 29.7% of firing variance
outcomes.notes: PC1 of the 1812 x 42 cue matrix (cueAnalysis.m) explains 29.73%; mean weights over the cue are danger 0.266, uncertainty 0.128, safety 0.006. The claims file's 47.1% on the Source Data inset is explained; the inset's 1812 rows equal the units' rows with the pre-cue baseline subtracted (the heat plot), not the matrix PCA was run on. Per animal PC1 explains 19.2 to 43.0% and is ordered in 9 of 10 animals (subject 9 has uncertainty 0.139 and safety 0.140).

outcomes.statement: PC1 firing information originated from nine clusters (k1 to k9), a minority of neurons (505 of 1812, 27.9%), with k1 and k2 contributing most per unit.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraphs 3 and 4; Figure 2c; Source Data Fig. 2c
outcomes.quote: PC1 firing information originated from nine clusters (k1–k9; Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. S5 ) composed of a minority of neurons (505/1812, 27.9%)
outcomes.notes: Under L1 the nine largest contributions per unit are k1 to k9 (505 units) under both s-a and s-b, with k1 and k2 the two largest; s-a, the script's shuffle (each row across its columns), gives every cluster's Source Data value within 0.0003. Under L2 (each of the 20 k-means solutions, numbered by contribution) the nine largest hold a median of 481 units over the seeds, within 505 +- 50.5; single seeds give 360 to 590, 13 of 20 within tolerance, and the best of 20 gives 411 (343 of them in L1's k1 to k9). The share of each animal's units in k1 to k9 ranges from 0.078 (subject 7) to 0.415 (subject 2).
deviations: L2 is judged on the median over the 20 seeds, the claims file's standard for a k-means result; the best of 20 is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: Clusters k1 to k9 showed shorter firing latencies after danger onset, and across all 21 clusters danger firing latency correlated negatively with the magnitude of PC1 contribution (R2 = 0.41, p = 0.0017).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 2d; Supplementary Methods, Danger firing latency
outcomes.quote: Clusters k1–k9 showed shorter firing latencies following danger onset, and across all clusters, danger firing latency negatively correlated with the magnitude of PC1 contribution ( R 2 = 0.41, p = 0.0017; Fig. 2d )
outcomes.notes: With the latency found within the 10-s cue as the Supplementary Methods say, the correlation across clusters is negative but weak and not significant (l-a r = -0.260, R2 = 0.067, p = 0.26; l-b R2 = 0.065, p = 0.26; with cluster totals, c-b, R2 = 0.122 and 0.104). Units of k1 to k9 do have shorter latencies than k10 to k21 (3571 against 4590 ms, l-a). 1778 units have a latency; Source Data lists 1498. The latencies differ from the paper's (k1 mean 4046 ms here, 182 ms in Source Data). A search from 2 s before onset keeping latencies after onset (a variant outside the criterion) gives 1458 units, k1 327 ms, and R2 = 0.640 (c-a, p = 1.4e-05), but it does not reproduce the Source Data latencies either; 413 of its values equal a Source Data value of the same cluster, against 513 for l-a. None of the paper's scripts computes the latency (findchangepts appears in none of them). On the Source Data latencies R2 is 0.508 (c-a) and 0.394 (c-b). The question of the window and of which units have no latency is for the paper's authors (findings).
deviations: Baseline subtraction and z-scoring are affine maps of the summed 1-ms spike counts, which leave a change point in mean unchanged, so l-a is computed on the summed spike counts of the four danger trials. findchangepts is implemented as one change in mean minimizing the residual sum of squares.

outcomes.statement: Clusters k1 to k9 separated from the rest by cluster-cluster cue firing correlations, forming a functional subnetwork within the larger brainstem network, with k3 the exception showing weak correlations with its fellow clusters.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 2e; Supplementary Methods, Correlated cluster firing
outcomes.quote: Clusters k1–k9 further separated themselves based on cluster-cluster cue firing correlations (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. S5 ), forming a functional subnetwork within the larger brainstem network. An exception was k3, which showed weak firing correlations with fellow clusters.
outcomes.notes: With r squared, the mean within k1 to k9 is 0.445 (42 columns) and 0.465 (36 columns), against 0.184 and 0.194 between k1 to k9 and k10 to k21, and k3 has the lowest mean with the other eight (0.225, 0.229). With r the within mean is also higher (0.129 against 0.068) but k8 is lowest (-0.516) because k7 and k8 decrease firing; the criterion names both and the claim holds under r squared. The script's 120-column variant gives the same with r squared except that k7 is lowest.

outcomes.statement: K1 and k2 were hubs of the cue subnetwork, with the greatest PC1 contributions, short danger latencies, and single-unit firing that correlated most strongly with the mean cue firing of their fellow subnetwork clusters.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 2f; Supplementary Methods, Hub identification with single unit x cluster correlations; Source Data Fig. 2f
outcomes.quote: K1 and k2 neurons showed indicators of a subnetwork hub ... Furthermore, k1 and k2 single-unit firing correlated most strongly with mean cue firing of their fellow subnetwork clusters

statistics.test: two-tailed independent samples t-test (means) and Levene's test (variances), between clusters

outcomes.notes: With danger firing over 14 intervals and r squared, k2 (0.503) and k1 (0.462) have the two highest means, within tolerance, but k1 does not exceed k3 (p = 0.42) or k4 (p = 0.12), and k2 does not exceed k3 (p = 0.014), at 0.05/7 or 0.05/8. With r, k1 and k3 are the two highest. The Source Data per-unit values equal r squared computed on the units' full 42-value cue rows (all three cues); with that measure k1 (0.424) and k2 (0.466) are the two highest and each exceeds all of k3 to k9 at both thresholds. Levene's tests are printed.
deviations: Assumed that the coefficient averaged is r squared, as the Methods call it ("seven separate correlation coefficients for each single unit (R2)") and as Source Data Fig. 2f, headed R2, holds; with r the claim would not be reproduced. The question is for the paper's authors, in the findings (paper_inconsistency).
The Methods' measure (danger firing) is the test; the Source Data values follow all three cues, shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: Neurons of every cue cluster were found in at least six brainstem regions, and subnetwork neurons, including the k1 and k2 hubs, were concentrated in the deep layer of the superior colliculus and the subdivisions of the periaqueductal gray.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 2g
outcomes.quote: Neurons from each cluster were observed in at least six brainstem regions (Fig. 2g ). Subnetwork neurons ... were concentrated in the deep layer of the superior colliculus and subdivisions of the periaqueductal gray.
outcomes.notes: Every cue cluster spans at least six regions (k3 six). The share in DPG, DpWh, DLPAG, LPAG and VLPAG is 0.436 (220/505) in the subnetwork and 0.612 (41/67) in k1 and k2, against 0.340 (445/1307) in the supranetwork.

outcomes.statement: Linear regression revealed distinct threat probability and fear behaviour signals across the 21 cue clusters, varying in time, with greatest signaling at onset (k5), at offset (k15), sustained over the cue (k10), or peaking mid cue (k6).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 3a
outcomes.quote: Linear regression revealed unique fear behavior and threat probability signaling across the 21 clusters (Fig. 3a ). Clusters showed considerable temporal variation in signaling prior to and following cue presentation, characterized by greatest signaling at onset (e.g., k5), offset (e.g., k15), sustained over cue presentation (e.g., k10), or even U-shaped signaling peaking mid cue (e.g., k6).
outcomes.notes: The script's regression (r-a with an intercept) gives betas equal to Source Data Fig. 3b middle. Two of four shapes hold under every reading; k5 peaks in the first cue second and k15 in the first second after the cue. K10's first cue second (0.77) is below half its maximum (1.69), so it is not sustained by the criterion's rule, and k6 peaks in cue second 5 (1.02) with its first cue second (0.60) above half that.

outcomes.statement: PCA of cluster beta weights showed PC1 (62.7% of signaling variance) to be a sustained behaviour signal peaking mid cue with lesser, opposing threat probability signaling, and PC2 (26.12%) a sustained threat probability signal peaking early in the cue with lesser behaviour signaling.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figure 3b; Source Data Fig. 3b
outcomes.quote: PC1 reflected a sustained behavior signal that peaked mid cue presentation, with lesser and opposing threat probability signaling (62.7% of signaling variance; Fig. 3b , middle). PC2 reflected a sustained threat probability signal that peaked during early cue presentation, with lesser behavior signaling (26.12% of signaling variance
outcomes.notes: The recomputed matrix equals Source Data Fig. 3b middle and gives 62.73% and 26.21%, with all shape conditions, also with the pre-cue baseline subtracted. Readings r-b and i-b give 72.00 and 15.79%, 57.07 and 27.94%, and 66.16 and 21.37%; L2 gives 63.08 and 25.04%.
deviations: The regression is the script's (cluster mean firing, mean member suppression ratio, with an intercept, cueAnalysis.m), which the Methods leave open.

outcomes.statement: Lesioning (shuffling) the cue subnetwork left the sustained behaviour signal intact but reduced threat probability signaling, most at cue onset, so sustained threat probability signaling depended more on the subnetwork.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 8; Figure 3c
outcomes.quote: Lesioning the subnetwork left sustained behavior signaling intact (Fig. 3c , PC1, middle), but reduced threat probability signaling, most apparent at cue onset (Fig. 3c , PC2, bottom).
outcomes.notes: With the script's lesion (s-c, giving 67.14 and 26.00% as the Source Data matrix does) PC1's mean behaviour weight over the cue is 0.264 after the subnetwork lesion (96% of the intact 0.274) and PC2's probability weight in the first cue second drops from 0.268 to 0.201, but the behaviour weight is not above the one after the supranetwork lesion (0.268). The paper's own Source Data matrices give the same. The difference is stable; over ten further runs of 1000 iterations the two weights average 0.2641 and 0.2678 (standard deviation 0.0001 each), and the subnetwork lesion's is above in none. v-b on s-c gives 49.49 and 21.00% and the same order (0.263 against 0.266); v-b on s-a gives 53.88 and 25.45%. Shuffling betas (s-a, s-b) meets every part. The criterion compares unit-norm weights; with loadings (a variant outside it) the behaviour loading is 0.709 against 0.680 (intact 0.756) and the PC2 probability loading falls from 0.479 to 0.335, so every part would hold. Whether loadings should be compared is asked of a reader (questions/strickland-2022.yaml).

outcomes.statement: Lesioning the cue supranetwork diminished the sustained behaviour signal and turned the sustained threat probability signal into a dynamic probability-to-behaviour signal, so sustained behaviour signaling depended more on the supranetwork.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 8; Figure 3d
outcomes.quote: By contrast, lesioning the supranetwork diminished sustained behavior signaling (Fig. 3d , PC1, middle), and shifted sustained threat probability signaling to dynamic, probability-to-behavior signaling (Fig. 3d , PC2, bottom).
outcomes.notes: With s-c (61.12 and 29.42%; Source Data 61.11 and 29.46%) PC1's mean behaviour weight is 0.268 against 0.274 intact, a small drop, and PC2's absolute probability weights peak in the second cue second, within the first half of the cue, and its behaviour weights in the tenth. With s-a and s-b the PC2 part fails. Over ten further runs of s-c the PC1 behaviour weight is 0.2678 (standard deviation 0.0001). With loadings (a variant) PC1's behaviour loading is 0.680 against 0.756 intact.

outcomes.statement: Subnetwork and supranetwork neurons were distributed throughout the brainstem, with subtle biases only for the subnetwork, to which the deep layer of the superior colliculus and the lateral periaqueductal gray contributed more.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 8; Figure 3e; Source Data Fig. 3e right
outcomes.quote: Subtle anatomical biases were only apparent for the cue subnetwork (Fig. 3e ), with the deep layer of the superior colliculus and the lateral subdivision of the periaqueductal gray (also sources of hub neurons) contributing more to the cue subnetwork.
outcomes.notes: LPAG (7.41) and DPG (5.93) have the two largest differentials, then DRD (3.13) and PMnR (2.53); all 21 equal Source Data Fig. 3e right. Under L2 LPAG and DPG are also the two largest.

outcomes.statement: K-means clustering of mean post-shock firing for the four trial types organized brainstem neurons into at least 11 functional clusters, of sizes from 46 to 322 (median 169).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 4b; Supplementary Methods, K-means clustering
outcomes.quote: K-means clustering for mean post-shock firing (4 trial types ... revealed brainstem neurons could be organized into at least 11 functional clusters (min size = 46, max = 322, and median = 169
outcomes.notes: Over 20 seeds the median largest (304.5) and median (161.0) sizes are within tolerance; the median smallest cluster is 29.0, against 46 +- 4.6, and single seeds give 1 to 58.
deviations: The script seeds MATLAB's generator (rng(1)), which cannot be repeated; 20 seeds are used.

outcomes.statement: PCA of post-shock firing of all 1812 neurons showed positive prediction error on top of shock responding as PC1 (17.7% of firing variance), with a larger weight for surprising shock on uncertainty trials than for predicted shock on danger trials, and no opposing negative error for surprising omission.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 4c
outcomes.quote: PCA for mean post-shock firing of all 1812 brainstem neurons revealed positive prediction error, on top of shock responding, to be the primary low-dimensional feature (PC1 explains 17.7% of firing variance ... The prediction error is "positive" because the PC1 weight for surprising shock delivery (on uncertainty trials) exceeded the PC1 weight for predicted shock (on danger trials). The prediction error is not "signed" because it did not include an opposing, negative error
outcomes.notes: PC1 of the 1812 x 80 outcome matrix (outcomeAnalysis.m) explains 17.68%, with mean weights uncertainty shock 0.194, danger 0.071, uncertainty omission -0.005 and safety -0.032. The Source Data Fig. 4c matrix (24.18%) is the heat-plot version with a baseline subtracted. Per animal, uncertainty shock has the largest weight in all 10 and danger exceeds safety in 9.

outcomes.statement: Outcome clusters k1 to k3 showed phasic firing changes after shock (k1 the greatest increases to surprising shock, k2 to predicted shock, k3 suppressed regardless of trial type) and by their correlations formed a phasic outcome network.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 10; Figure 4b and 4d
outcomes.quote: K1 neurons showed the greatest, phasic firing increases to surprising shock, and k2 neurons greatest, phasic firing increases to predicted shock, while k3 neurons physically suppressed firing following shock irrespective of trial type (Fig. 4b , left column). Cluster-cluster firing correlations revealed k1–k3 formed a phasic outcome network
outcomes.notes: Under L1, k1 to k3 have higher temporal indices than every one of k6 to k9 (t-a and t-b); in the first second k1 uncertainty shock 2.58 > danger 1.59 > 0, k2 danger 2.85 > uncertainty shock 1.44 > 0, and k3 below 0 on both. The network part fails with the Pearson correlation the criterion names; the mean r among k1 to k3 is -0.329 against 0.008 with k4 to k11, as k3 is anticorrelated with k1 and k2 (r = -0.85, -0.74). With r squared, the coefficient the Methods name ("Pearson's correlation coefficient (R2)") and outcomeAnalysis.m plots, it is 0.539 against 0.076 and the claim would be reproduced; whether the criterion should allow r squared, as the fig2e criterion does, is asked of a reader (questions/strickland-2022.yaml). Under L2 the phasic network part holds in 10 of 20 seeds with r and 15 with r squared.

outcomes.statement: Outcome clusters k6 to k9 showed sustained firing changes after surprising shock (k6 selectively inhibited, k7 and k8 sustained increases maximal to surprising shock) and by their correlations formed a tonic outcome network.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 10; Figure 4b and 4d
outcomes.quote: K6–k9 neurons showed sustained firing changes following surprising shock (Fig. 4b , right column). K6 neurons selectively inhibited firing to surprising shock, while k7 and k8 neurons showed sustained firing increases that were maximal to surprising shock. Cluster-cluster firing correlations revealed k6–k9 formed a tonic outcome network
outcomes.notes: Under L1, k6's mean firing to uncertainty shock (-0.88) is below 0 and below its other trial types; k7 (0.82) and k8 (0.31) are above 0 and highest for uncertainty shock, and both are sustained. The network part fails with the Pearson correlation the criterion names; the mean r among k6 to k9 is -0.250 against 0.000 with the other seven (k6 and k9 are correlated, r = 0.67, and both are anticorrelated with k7 and k8, r = -0.88, -0.58, -0.60 and -0.79). With r squared it is 0.505 against 0.110 and the claim would be reproduced; the coefficient is asked of a reader, as for fig4b-phasic-network. Under L2 the tonic network part holds in none of 20 seeds with r and in all 20 with r squared.

outcomes.statement: Within the phasic outcome network, PC1 (37.0% of firing variance) was equivalent phasic shock firing on danger and uncertainty trials; within the tonic outcome network, PC1 (29.2%) was selective firing to surprising shock with opposing firing to safety.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 10; Figure 4e
outcomes.quote: Network-specific PCA for post-shock firing revealed equivalent and phasic shock firing on danger and uncertainty trials to be the primary low-dimensional feature of the phasic outcome network (explaining 37.0% of firing variance; Fig. 4e , left). PCA further revealed selective firing to surprising shock, and opposing firing to safety, to be the primary low-dimensional feature of the tonic outcome network (explaining 29.2% of firing variance
outcomes.notes: 265 phasic and 613 tonic units. Phasic PC1 first-second weights are danger 0.410 and uncertainty shock 0.424, each more than twice their late means; tonic PC1 is largest for uncertainty shock (0.202) and negative for safety (-0.078). The Source Data matrices give the same.

outcomes.statement: In the phasic outcome network, k1 and k2 single-unit firing correlated better with the population firing of their fellow clusters than k3 did; in the tonic network, k6, the cluster decreasing firing to surprising shock, was the hub, correlating most strongly with its fellow clusters.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 11; Figure 4f; Supplementary Methods, Hub identification
outcomes.quote: Within the phasic outcome network, k1 and k2 single-unit firing was better correlated with population firing of their fellow network clusters than were k3 neurons (Fig. 4f , left) ... K6 neurons were a hub for the tonic outcome network. K6 neuron firing, the cluster decreasing firing to surprising shock, correlated most strongly with population firing of their fellow tonic outcome clusters

statistics.test: two-tailed independent samples t-test and Levene's test, between clusters

outcomes.notes: With the script's measure (r squared, outcomeAnalysis.m), whose per-unit values equal Source Data Fig. 4f as a set, k1 (0.274) and k2 (0.260) exceed k3 (0.148; p = 3.6e-12 and 9.8e-08) and k6 (0.264) exceeds k7 (0.197), k8 (0.157) and k9 (0.119), all below 0.05/3 and 0.05/6. With r the phasic part holds and k6 has the lowest tonic mean. The Methods' networks (1-5, 7-10) are shown. Source Data Fig. 4f right labels 171 rows as k7 and 111 as k8; the rows labelled k7 hold the 111 k7 values and 60 k8 values, as the script's hard-coded labels (outcomeAnalysis.m line 936) give, so only the labels are swapped. The tests use the units' own clusters.
deviations: Bonferroni over the pairs within each network (3 and 6), a choice the claims file leaves to the count of tests.

outcomes.statement: Phasic outcome neurons were more common at the axis extremes (periaqueductal gray subregions, dorsal raphe and paramedian raphe), while tonic outcome neurons, most strikingly the k6 hub, were distributed throughout the brainstem.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 11; Figure 4g
outcomes.quote: Phasic outcome neurons were more common at axis extremes ... Tonic outcome neurons were distributed throughout the brainstem, a pattern most striking for k6 hub neurons.
outcomes.notes: 0.600 of phasic and 0.594 of tonic units are in the axis-extreme regions (difference 0.006, chi-square p = 0.92); the tonic network spans 20 regions and the phasic 17; k6 spans 17 against 10 to 19 for the other clusters. The effect is as small as on the paper's own values.

outcomes.statement: Regression revealed distinct shock and prediction error signals across the 11 outcome clusters; k1 neurons transiently signaled both sensory shock and prediction error, while k6 neurons signaled only error.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 12; Figure 5a
outcomes.quote: First, cluster-specific linear regression revealed unique shock and prediction error signals across the 11 outcome clusters (Fig. 5a ). For example, k1 neurons transiently signaled both sensory shock and prediction error, while k6 neurons exclusively signaled error.
outcomes.notes: Under all four readings k1's shock and prediction error betas peak in the first 2 s and stay below half that from 5 to 10 s, and k6's mean absolute prediction error beta is 12.3 times its mean absolute shock beta (8.9 without an intercept).

outcomes.statement: PCA of outcome cluster beta weights showed opposing sensory shock and prediction error signals as PC1 (53.7% of signaling variance) and dynamic sensory shock to prediction error signaling as PC2 (33.4%).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 12; Figure 5b; Source Data Fig. 5b
outcomes.quote: PCA for shock and prediction error beta coefficients across all clusters (therefore all brainstem neurons) revealed opposing sensory shock and prediction error signals to be the primary low-dimensional feature (PC1, 53.7% of signaling variance; Fig. 5b , middle). PC2 reflected dynamic, sensory shock to prediction error signaling (33.4% of signaling variance
outcomes.notes: The recomputed betas equal Source Data Fig. 5b middle, with prediction error in columns 1 to 20 and shock in 21 to 40 (outcomeRegression.m), the reverse of the Methods' layout; the shapes are tested on the betas of each regressor. L2 gives 47.80 and 30.92% (PC1 out of tolerance, PC2 within it) with the same shapes.

outcomes.statement: Lesioning the phasic outcome network left signaling dominated by sustained prediction error (80.0% of signaling variance), with residual sustained shock (16.8%), so rapid sensory shock signaling depended on the phasic network.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 13; Figure 5c
outcomes.quote: Lesioning the phasic outcome network (using a PCA lesion approach identical to the cue networks) left signaling dominated by sustained prediction error (80.0% of signaling variance; Fig. 5c , middle), while the residual reflected sustained shock (16.8% of signaling variance
outcomes.notes: The script's lesion (firing permuted across trial rows before regression, s-d) gives 79.99 and 16.81% with one permutation for all intervals and 79.98 and 16.82% with one per interval; all shapes hold. Shuffling betas gives 76.50 and 20.07% (s-a) and 78.59 and 17.89% (s-b).

outcomes.statement: Lesioning the tonic outcome network left opposing, phasic sensory shock and prediction error signaling as PC1 (61.3% of signaling variance) and dynamic sensory shock to prediction error as PC2 (29.8%), similar to that of all neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 13; Figure 5d
outcomes.quote: By contrast, lesioning the tonic outcome network emphasized opposing, phasic sensory shock and prediction error signaling (61.3% of signaling variance; Fig. 5d , middle). Residual signaling reflected dynamic, sensory shock to prediction error (29.8% of signaling variance
outcomes.notes: With s-d, 61.18 and 29.88% (one permutation for all intervals) or 61.24 and 29.80%; PC1 has opposing shock and prediction error weights peaking in the first 2 s, and PC2 correlates with the intact PC2 at r = 0.895. Shuffling betas gives 53.45% (s-a) and 60.93% (s-b) for PC1.

outcomes.statement: Anatomical biases for phasic and tonic outcome network neurons were absent.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 13; Figure 5e; Source Data Fig. 5e
outcomes.quote: Anatomical biases for phasic and tonic outcome network neurons were absent (Fig. 5e ).
outcomes.notes: With phasic read as k1 to k5 (p-b), the reading Source Data Fig. 5e uses (679 units), the largest differential is 4.48 points (MnR), at the criterion's limit, and every value equals Source Data. This reading cannot fail once the data match Source Data, since the threshold is the largest Source Data value of the same quantity. With phasic as k1 to k3 (p-a), the phasic network of the Results, the largest is 9.82 (PMnR), above 1.5 x 4.48, which would not reproduce it. With network labels permuted among the units of the two networks (1000 times, a variant) the 95th percentile of the largest differential is 5.88 (p-a) and 4.64 (p-b); 9.82 is reached in 0.001 of permutations and 4.48 in 0.058. The chi-square of region by network, a variant, gives p = 0.039 (p-b) and 3e-05 (p-a). The threshold and the phasic set are asked of a reader (questions/strickland-2022.yaml).
deviations: Assumed reading p-b, the computation behind the paper's Fig. 5e (Source Data), because a claim of absence is judged on the paper's own test as written (protocol, reader step 3); the Results define the phasic network as k1 to k3 (p-a), under which the claim would not be reproduced, and p-a is shown.

outcomes.statement: Membership in cue networks did not influence membership in outcome networks; neither the phasic (85/265, 32.1%) nor the tonic (159/613, 25.9%) outcome neurons differed from the 27.9% expected in the cue subnetwork.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 14; Supplementary Methods, Relationship between cue network and outcome network membership
outcomes.quote: Chi-squared testing found neither the phasic outcome neurons (85/265, 32.1%; χ 2 = 2.27, p = 0.13) nor the tonic outcome neurons (159/613, 25.9%; χ 2 = 1.17, p = 0.28) differed from the expected proportion of 27.9%.

statistics.about: phasic outcome units in the cue subnetwork against 27.9%
tonic outcome units in the cue subnetwork against 27.9%

outcomes.notes: Under L1, 85 of 265 phasic and 159 of 613 tonic units are in the cue subnetwork; against 0.279 chi-square 2.30 (p = 0.13) and 1.17 (p = 0.28); 2 x 2 tests p = 0.10 and 0.19. Under L2 the result depends on the clustering; over the 20 seeds (cue and outcome solutions of the same seed) the median goodness-of-fit p is 0.048 (phasic) and 0.011 (tonic), and neither goodness-of-fit test has p < 0.05 in 4 of 20 seeds. The outcome is judged on the paper's own membership (L1), the networks whose counts the claim gives.
deviations: Assumed that the outcome is judged on L1, the paper's own membership (Source Data Fig. 2f and 4f), whose counts (85 of 265, 159 of 613) are those the claim and Results paragraph 14 give. The criterion says only that results are reported under L1 and L2. Judged on the median over the 20 L2 seeds, the goodness-of-fit p values (0.048 and 0.011) would make the claim not reproduced.

findings.statement: 204 of the 1812 unit files hold repeated spike times (9289 repeats in all). The paper's cubeScript.m counts spikes with intersect(), which keeps each time once, so the cube's counts leave the repeats out.

The data set holds no cluster membership. The paper's k-means clusters come from MATLAB's kmeans after rng(1), relabelled by hand-written maps in cueAnalysis.m and outcomeAnalysis.m, so they cannot be regenerated outside MATLAB; they can be recovered only from the paper's Source Data workbook, whose cluster sheets every unit matches exactly.

The cube's anatomy.region holds region names as MATLAB string objects, which cannot be read outside MATLAB. The region numbers need the list in cubeScript.m, and the analysis scripts renumber 35 units from region 21 (CIC) to DpWh, saying the cube assigned them in error, and merge regions 11 and 24 into x/scp. The units of anatomy.x, y and z are not stated.

In session js10030220, 19 unit files share one set of event times, while 2 others (spk0009, spk0044) and 1 more (spk0049) carry cue and poke times that differ from them by an amount growing over the session to about 0.28 and 0.30 s. The cube uses each file's own times.
Session js27101920 has 5 shock times; no shock is recorded on its first danger trial (row 1). All other 72 sessions have 6 shocks, 12.0 s after cue onset on rows 1 to 6.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module bst3.py and the claims file, with the paper's full text and Source Data under paper/. The verifier tested the helpers on synthetic inputs (change_point, mixed_anova_cue_by_group, pca, pc1_percent, shuffle_rows, differential, suppression_ratios) and checked the archive's file list. It did not see the attempt record.

disagreements.reason: Under L1, k1 to k9 are the nine largest, k1 = 0.1214 and k2 = 0.1129, matching Source Data to 4e-4. Under L2, the criterion's "must" part fails, the nine largest clusters hold 411 units, outside 505 +- 50.5. The L2 labels come from one seed, the best of 20, while the claims file's standard is the median over 20 seeds, so the L2 total of 411 rests on a single solution.

Phasic indices (t-a and t-b) and the k1, k2, k3 profiles hold. With the criterion's Pearson r, the network part fails, within -0.329 against 0.008 with the rest. It passes only under r squared, which the notebook runs without stating it as an assumption for this claim. The Methods passage does allow r squared; this is a claims-file inconsistency, since it allows r and r squared for fig2e but not here.
The k6 to k8 profiles and the sustained test hold. With r, the network part fails, within -0.250 against 0.000. It passes only under r squared.

Under p-b (k1-k5), the largest differential is 4.48, exactly Source Data, but the threshold is taken from that same quantity, so this cannot fail; this is a design flaw in the claims file. Under p-a (the Results' phasic network k1-k3), PMnR is -9.82 and MnR -9.29, more than 6.72. The verifier gave partially because the two readings disagree, its own call and not one of the criterion's levels.

verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook of the first revision, with its conclusions and summary, the helper module bst3.py, the claims file, the attempt record, the README and the questions file, with the paper's full text and Source Data under paper/.

paper_notes.statement: Supplementary Table 1 lists 75 recording sessions (8 for subject 5 and 10 for subject 10); the Results and the data set have 73 (7 and 9).

The Source Data danger latencies (Fig. 2d) do not follow the Supplementary Methods' search within the 10-s cue (k1 mean 182 ms there, 4046 ms with the stated method), and 1498 of 1812 units have one, by a rule not stated. A search from 2 s before cue onset does not reproduce them either, and none of the scripts in the data set computes the latency. Which window was searched, how the 1-ms firing was built, and which units were left out? With the stated method the latency does not correlate with PC1 contribution (R2 = 0.067).

For the cue hubs (Fig. 2f) the Supplementary Methods correlate danger firing over 14 intervals, but the Source Data per-unit values are squared correlations of the full 42-value cue rows (all three cues). Was r or r squared averaged, and over which cues? With danger firing the k1 hub does not exceed k3 or k4.

The Methods call the cluster correlations "Pearson's correlation coefficient (R2)" and the scripts plot r squared. Is the network separation of Fig. 2e and 4d judged on r squared? With r, k3 is anticorrelated with k1 and k2, k6 and k9 with k7 and k8, and the outcome networks do not separate. Whether the claims file's criteria for the outcome networks should allow r squared is also asked of a reader (questions/strickland-2022.yaml).

The Supplementary Methods lay out the outcome beta matrix with shock in intervals 1 to 20 and prediction error in 21 to 40, as a 21-cluster matrix; outcomeRegression.m and Source Data Fig. 5b to 5d hold prediction error first, for 11 clusters.
Source Data Fig. 4f right labels 171 units as k7 and 111 as k8, as outcomeAnalysis.m hard-codes them, where the Figure 4b sheets and the clustering have 111 units in k7 and 171 in k8.

The normalization in cubeScript.m (1-s, 500-ms and 250-ms bins z-scored separately over the 40 s from 10 s before cue onset, baseline rounded down) differs from the Supplementary Methods (250-ms bins from 20 s before to 20 s after the cue, averaged into larger intervals); only the script's normalization reproduces the paper's values. The lesion scripts shuffle firing of k1 to k9, k1 to k3 and k6 to k9 before regression, where the Methods shuffle the betas of clusters 1 to 8.

Source Data Fig. 2c inset and Fig. 4c hold the units' rows with a pre-cue baseline subtracted (the heat-plot data), not the matrices whose PCA gives the reported 29.7% and 17.7%; PCA of those sheets gives 47.1% and 24.2%.

entries.name: strickland-2022
entries.title: Brainstem networks for threat probability and prediction error (Strickland and McDannald 2022)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Strickland and McDannald (2022) on CRCNS data set bst-3, which holds 1812 brainstem single units recorded with Neuropixels in ten rats during probabilistic fear discrimination, the cube file of binned and normalized firing built from them, and the paper's MATLAB scripts. It checks the behaviour, the unit counts, the k-means clusters and their PCA, the regression and lesion analyses of threat probability, behaviour, shock and prediction error signals, and the anatomy of the networks, with the paper's own cluster membership taken from its Source Data.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Strickland and McDannald (2022) from CRCNS bst-3
